name: Royal jelly
short: A case series describes asthma and anaphylaxis after royal jelly; a survey's background note says it has also been linked with death. One case report describes bleeding and raised INR with warfarin.
text: A case series described asthma, in some cases with anaphylaxis, in seven people after they ate royal jelly, and testing showed these were true IgE-mediated allergic reactions. The abstract of a later survey states as background, without giving a source or details, that royal jelly consumption had recently been linked with acute asthma, anaphylaxis and death; this is a background statement, not a finding of the survey. In that survey of 1472 hospital employees in Hong Kong, 461 had taken royal jelly and nine reported adverse reactions (urticaria, eczema, rhinitis and acute asthma); about 7% of those skin-tested (176 survey respondents and 300 asthma clinic patients, with a similar proportion in each group) reacted to royal jelly, and all but one of these were allergic to other common allergens, so people with allergies appear to be at higher risk of sensitisation, although the authors said the link between use, skin-test results and clinical reactions remains to be defined. For interactions, a single case report describes an 87-year-old man on long-term warfarin who had blood in his urine and an INR of 6.88 one week after starting royal jelly; the authors judged an interaction the most probable explanation and knew of no earlier such reports.
